title: Who may see this file?
teaches: Permissions as relation tuples, the "new enemy" problem and consistency tokens, and answering ten million checks a second

blocks.text: In July 2019, at the USENIX Annual Technical Conference in Renton, Washington, Ruoming Pang and fourteen colleagues from Google described Zanzibar, the service that decides who may see what across Google's products.[^burrows] Drive, Calendar, Cloud, Maps, Photos and YouTube all asked it whether a given user had a specific permission on a target object, many times for every page. The paper reported more than two trillion stored permissions, more than ten million checks a second, 95% of them answered in under 10 ms, and availability above 99.999% over three years.

Before Zanzibar, each product kept its own access control lists in its own format. That works until products share resources, such as a Drive file attached to a Calendar event, a YouTube video shared with a Google group, or a Cloud project whose members come from a company's directory. Each product then has to evaluate the others' rules, and two products can give different answers about the same person and the same file.

Zanzibar's design relies on **explicit engineering trade-offs**. The builders made three choices that each incur a specific cost: centralising permissions in one shared service, which every product then depends on for availability; requiring the client to specify its consistency bounds per request, rather than enforcing global strict serializability; and serving answers from caches and stale snapshots wherever consistency allows. In this lesson, we will examine these three choices and the operational cost of each.

Zanzibar stores every permission as a **relation tuple** consisting of an object, a relation, and a user, written `object#relation@user`. For example, `doc:readme#owner@user:alice` says Alice owns the readme. The user field can also hold a set of users, called a **userset**, written as an object and a relation: `doc:readme#viewer@group:eng#member` says every member of the eng group may view the document, and `group:eng#member@user:bob` makes Bob a member. Groups can hold other groups, so membership forms a directed graph, and an access check is a graph traversal.

Some permissions follow from others, and storing all implied permissions explicitly would waste space and drift out of step. Instead, each namespace has a short configuration of **userset rewrite rules** that define how relations derive from one another. For a document, an owner is also an editor, an editor is also a viewer, and a viewer of the document's parent folder is a viewer of the document. A call to `check(doc:plan, viewer, user:bob)` evaluates whether Bob is a direct viewer, an editor, an owner, or a viewer of the folder, traversing recursively through each parent group and folder. The client makes a single call that returns a boolean.

We can estimate the storage capacity required from the tuple count. Two trillion tuples, at roughly 50 bytes each for the object, relation, user and timestamp, take 100 TB of raw storage. That is more than a single machine holds, though modest for a distributed database. Zanzibar stores its tuples in Spanner, the database from lesson 20, so every write is a transaction with a commit timestamp, and every read evaluates against a specific snapshot timestamp. A client product writes tuples when its users share or unshare resources, and reads them by issuing check requests.

One alternative is for each product to cache its own copy of the access lists for 60 seconds, which introduces a consistency failure we will examine in the next section. Another alternative is traversing every nested group in the database at request time, which fails on latency: checking a document shared with five levels of nested groups requires five or more sequential database reads, adding tens of milliseconds on every cache miss.

The paper calls one consistency failure the **new enemy problem**. Suppose Alice removes Bob from a shared folder because she is about to upload a document he must not see, and then adds the document. If the access check for Bob reads from a snapshot taken before his removal, Bob can read the new document. Alice's ordering of operations protects her only if the check evaluates against a snapshot that includes the removal; a snapshot from before the removal shows Bob still in the folder, regardless of when the document arrived. Run the simulation below without a consistency token, then enable the fix.

blocks.task: Play it without a zookie and watch Bob get in; then carry a zookie and play it through

blocks.text: Nothing in the failing run is a software bug in any individual component. Spanner committed the removal, and Zanzibar answered the check accurately for the snapshot timestamp it selected. The failure happens because the client did not specify that the check required a snapshot at least as recent as the permission state the new document depended on. If a product caches access lists locally and refreshes them once a minute, it exposes the same vulnerability for up to 60 seconds after every revocation.

Zanzibar prevents this using a consistency token the paper calls a **zookie**. When a product saves new content, it makes a *content-change check*, which is an ordinary check verifying that the writer has permission to modify the resource (for example, that Alice may edit the folder) that also returns a zookie. The zookie is an opaque byte string containing a Spanner timestamp at least as late as every permission change committed before the save. The product stores the zookie alongside the new version of the content. When any user later asks to read that content, the product passes the stored zookie with the check request, instructing Zanzibar to evaluate the check at a snapshot no older than the zookie's timestamp. Spanner's external consistency guarantee from lesson 20 makes this safe: because the access removal committed before the content-change check began, its commit timestamp is smaller than the zookie's timestamp, so any snapshot at or after the zookie's timestamp includes the removal.

Evaluating every check at the latest Spanner timestamp would also prevent the new enemy problem, and it is the simplest design to reason about. The penalty is high read latency and low cache hit rates. Reading at the latest timestamp requires contacting each Spanner shard's Paxos leader, which may sit on another continent 50 ms to 100 ms away, and a check evaluated at a unique, brand-new timestamp cannot hit an existing cache entry. Most checks do not require strict freshness: if Bob opens a document whose permissions last changed a month ago, a snapshot from 10 seconds ago returns the exact same result.

So the freshness is stated by the client, per request. A check with a zookie gets a snapshot at least that new. A check without one lets Zanzibar choose, and it chooses a snapshot slightly in the past: one that the nearest replica already holds, so no round trip to a leader, and one shared with other checks, so their answers can be cached and reused.[^quantise] Content changes are rare beside reads, so few checks pay for freshness and the rest are served locally. Rounding to a granularity of g seconds adds at most g seconds of staleness: with 10-second rounding, a check without a zookie may see permissions up to about ten seconds old, and checks within each ten seconds share cache entries.

This protocol trades consistency against latency and database load, letting the client service choose the bound per request because only the client knows when content changes. The cost of this design is implementation complexity for every client engineering team: each product must store a zookie alongside every version of its content and pass it back on reads. If a client team forgets to pass the zookie, they reintroduce the new enemy problem for their users. Zanzibar cannot detect a missing zookie; it can only evaluate the timestamp constraints it receives. Legacy content saved before a product integrated zookies has no token, so checks against it fall back to the default staleness window until the content is modified and receives a token. Client teams can only catch a missing zookie through their own integration tests, such as a test that revokes access, writes content, and immediately checks permissions.

blocks.title: What a zookie carries
points: An opaque token containing a Spanner timestamp, returned by the content-change check when the client saves content.
The evaluation constraint: Zanzibar must evaluate the check at a database snapshot no older than the token's timestamp.
It contains no access control data itself; it only sets a lower bound on the snapshot timestamp.
Checks that do not carry a zookie are free to evaluate against older, quantised snapshots stored in local replicas and caches.

blocks.text: The throughput and latency targets dictate the serving architecture. Serving 10 million checks a second across 10,000 servers averages 1,000 checks a second per server, and a 95th-percentile latency budget of 10 ms leaves room for at most one or two Spanner reads on the critical path: reading from a local Spanner replica takes a few milliseconds, while contacting a Paxos leader across an ocean takes 50 ms to 100 ms.[^servers] Most checks must therefore be answered from memory. Each check server caches the results of its Spanner reads and intermediate sub-checks, keyed by object, relation, user and snapshot timestamp.

A distributed cache's hit rate depends on how requests are routed. If load balancers send checks to servers at random, requests for a popular document land on every server, and every server caches a duplicate copy of the same popular results. Instead, Zanzibar routes each check and sub-check using consistent hashing on the object ID (as in lesson 5), so all answers for a given object live in a single server's memory, and the fleet's caches partition the keyspace rather than duplicating it. Compare the two routing strategies in the simulation below, then increase the popularity skew.

blocks.caption: Products send checks on 2,000 objects, whose popularity falls off as 1/rank to a power s, through four check servers that each cache answers for 100 objects. Misses read from Spanner. Slow motion; illustrative numbers.
blocks.task: Compare the routings Any server and By object, then raise the skew to 1.2 or more and choose By object, hot ones spread

blocks.text: Routing by object raises the hit rate, here from about 63% to 80% at s = 1.0, but it puts every check on the most popular object on one server. At s = 1.4 the most checked object alone takes about a third of all checks, so the server that owns it carries nearly half of all checks while the others carry under a fifth each, and its queue sets the latency for everyone routed to it. The drawing's fix is the general one: notice the few hottest objects and let any server answer them, which costs almost no hits because those few fit in every cache.

The Zanzibar paper details several mechanisms to mitigate hot spots and tail latency. Each check server maintains a **lock table** tracking in-flight Spanner reads and sub-checks; if 1,000 identical checks arrive concurrently on a cache miss, 999 wait on the lock table for the single database read to return, preventing the thundering herd problem from lesson 15. For hot objects, Zanzibar prefetches and caches all tuples for that object in a single batch read, and distributes those cached entries across all servers rather than hashing to one. Finally, slow Spanner reads and remote sub-checks are **hedged**: if a request takes longer than a threshold, the server sends a duplicate request to another replica (as in lesson 9) and uses whichever response returns first.

Deeply nested groups require a dedicated indexing system. An index service called **Leopard** maintains flattened group representations, updated continuously from the tuple changelog: it maps each user to the groups they belong to, and each group to the ancestor or descendant groups nested with it at any depth. To check whether a user belongs to a target group, the server fetches the user's group set and the target group's nested set and tests whether the two sorted sets intersect in memory, replacing five sequential database hops with a single set intersection.[^leopard]

parts.title: One service that everyone depends on

blocks.text: Centralising authorization gives every Google product consistent answers for any user and resource, and concentrates the engineering effort of caching, indexing and replication in one team. The operational risk is that Zanzibar becomes a critical dependency for every product. A service that cannot verify permissions must fail closed and refuse to serve data, so a global Zanzibar outage takes down every dependent product simultaneously. That dependency is why Zanzibar targets 99.999% availability, which permits just over five minutes of downtime a year, and why the paper devotes as much attention to tail-latency mitigations as to the tuple data model.

Adopting Zanzibar imposes three other constraints on client products. First, teams must model their authorization rules strictly as relation tuples and userset rewrites, which fits document sharing and group hierarchies naturally but struggles to express dynamic attribute-based rules such as "allow access only during business hours". Second, every permission change is a cross-region Spanner transaction taking tens of milliseconds, which works only because permission writes are orders of magnitude rarer than permission checks. Third, client engineers must store and pass zookies on every content change and read, a protocol invariant that Zanzibar can document but cannot verify.

Engineers outside Google have since built open-source systems based on the Zanzibar paper. SpiceDB from Authzed, and OpenFGA, started at Auth0 and later donated to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, both implement relation tuples, userset rewrite rules and consistency tokens.[^descendants] Both systems expose the same consistency-latency trade-off in their APIs, letting callers request strict evaluation against the latest database state or accept cached evaluations from recent snapshots.

blocks.caption: Seven questions on permissions at scale
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Alice removes Bob from a folder, then adds a secret document to it. Bob can open the document. Which explanation is best?
choices: The removal had not been committed when the document was added, because Zanzibar writes permission changes in the background
Bob's check was answered from a snapshot taken before the removal, which nothing required to be newer
Bob's client cached the folder's access list from his last visit, and the document inherited the cached list
items.why: Every component operated accurately for the snapshot timestamp it used. The failure occurred because the client did not constrain the check to evaluate at a snapshot at least as recent as the permission state the new document depended on, which is the new enemy problem.

items.ask: What does a zookie hold, and what does Zanzibar do with it?
choices: A copy of the access list as it stood when the content was saved, which the check uses instead of reading Spanner
A signed statement that the user was allowed at a certain time, valid for a fixed period afterwards
A point in time no earlier than the last permission change before the save, and Zanzibar must not answer from older data
items.why: The zookie sets a lower bound on the snapshot timestamp used to evaluate the check. It does not store permissions or grant access itself; Zanzibar still evaluates the request against the tuples stored in Spanner.

items.ask: Why does Zanzibar not simply answer every check at the newest snapshot?
choices: Fresh data must come from each shard's leader, perhaps on another continent, and a fresh snapshot cannot be served from cache
Spanner forbids reading at the newest timestamp until commit wait has passed, which would add whole seconds to every single check
The newest snapshot may include half of a transaction that is still committing, so answers could change
items.why: Reading at the latest timestamp requires round trips to Paxos leaders and bypasses existing cache entries. Most checks inspect resources whose permissions have not changed in the last few seconds, so evaluating against a slightly older, cached snapshot returns the exact same result at much lower latency.

items.ask: Each product caches access lists for 60 seconds to save calls to the permission service. What follows?
choices: Nothing that matters, because a removal and a new document within the same minute are too rare to plan for
For up to a minute after someone is removed, they can see content added in that minute
Checks become slower, because each product must also refresh its cache in the request path
items.why: Because the cached access list is older than the removal, any document added right after the removal is checked against the stale list. This leaves the new enemy vulnerability open for the entire 60-second time-to-live (TTL) window after every revocation.

items.ask: Ten check servers each cache answers for 100,000 objects. Popularity is steep. What does routing each check by its object, rather than to any server, change?
choices: The caches together hold about a million distinct objects instead of the same 100,000 ten times, so far fewer checks miss
Each server's cache holds fewer objects, because consistent hashing reserves space on each server for the others' keys
Nothing about hits, since every cache still holds 100,000 objects; it only spreads load more evenly over the servers
items.why: With random routing, every server caches the same popular objects. Routing by object partitions the keyspace so each server caches a distinct subset of objects, increasing the effective cache capacity across the fleet tenfold. The downside is that all requests for a single hot object land on a single server.

items.ask: A public document is checked 50,000 times a second, and routing by object sends every check for it to one server. Which response fits?
choices: Give that server a larger cache, so the document's answers stay cached
Let any server answer checks for the few hottest objects
Route every check to any server again, because routing by object only raises the hit rate for objects that are rarely checked
items.why: The hot object is already cached; the problem is the load on one server. Spreading only the hottest few costs almost no hit rate, and merging identical in-flight checks stops a burst of misses becoming a burst of reads.

items.ask: Groups contain groups up to six levels deep. Why does Zanzibar keep a separate index for group membership?
choices: Spanner cannot store tuples whose user is a group, so nested membership has to live in another system
Without it, a check walks the nesting one read after another, and six sequential reads overrun a 10 ms budget
The index lets products change group membership without writing tuples, which saves a transaction on every change
items.why: Each level of group nesting requires a database read that depends on the result of the previous read. Maintaining an in-memory index of flattened group memberships turns a sequential graph traversal into a single set intersection.

summary: **Store permissions as relation tuples.** Express access rules as `object#relation@user`, where the user can be a userset such as `group:eng#member` to represent group and folder inheritance.

**Derive implied permissions from rewrite rules rather than storing copies.** Namespace rules define how relations derive (an owner is an editor, and a folder viewer can view its files), and Zanzibar evaluates them during a check.
**Size the storage engine from the tuple count.** Two trillion tuples at roughly 50 bytes each require 100 TB of storage, which Zanzibar distributes across Spanner.

**The new enemy problem occurs when a revoked user sees newer content.** It happens whenever an access check evaluates against a database snapshot older than a permission change that the new content depended on.

**A zookie records a Spanner timestamp from when content was modified.** Checks carrying a zookie must evaluate at a snapshot at least as recent as that timestamp, while checks without one can use older, cached snapshots.

**Require the client to specify its freshness bound.** Reading the latest state requires round trips to Paxos leaders and bypasses caches, so only requests that depend on a recent change should pay that latency cost.

**Route checks by object ID with consistent hashing to partition the cache.** Each server caches a distinct share of objects rather than duplicating popular ones, at the cost of concentrating traffic for a hot object on a single machine.

**Add dedicated mechanisms for hot spots and deep group hierarchies.** Coalesce identical in-flight checks in a lock table, spread the hottest objects across all servers, and evaluate deep group nesting with an in-memory flattened set index.
**Centralising permissions makes the authorization service a critical dependency.** Providing consistent answers across every product requires engineering the shared service for 99.999% availability.

burrows.title: An author from lesson 11
burrows.text: Among the authors was Mike Burrows, who designed Chubby, the lock service of lesson 11. Zanzibar uses Chubby to store its namespace configurations and manage coarse-grained coordination.

quantise.title: Rounding the snapshot
quantise.text: The paper describes quantising the evaluation timestamps of checks without a zookie to a coarse granularity (such as 1 second or 10 seconds), so that checks arriving close together share a single snapshot timestamp and reuse the same cache entries. Cache entries keyed by an exact microsecond timestamp would almost never be hit twice.

servers.title: The serving fleet
servers.text: The paper put Zanzibar's serving fleet at more than 10,000 servers across several dozen clusters around the world, reading from Spanner databases replicated in more than 30 locations. Those figures are from 2019.

leopard.title: Leopard
leopard.text: Leopard builds its initial index from an offline snapshot of the tuples in Spanner and keeps the in-memory sets current by consuming a live changelog stream of tuple writes.

descendants.title: Open-source descendants
descendants.text: Authzed released SpiceDB in September 2021; Auth0, by then part of Okta, released OpenFGA in June 2022. SpiceDB calls its consistency token a ZedToken. Both systems let developers define userset rewrite rules in a schema DSL modelled on Zanzibar's namespace configurations.
